text: Which description identifies a compound?
options: Different elements bonded in a fixed ratio
Two substances physically mixed in any ratio
A substance separated by simple filtration
scheme: Compounds consist of chemically bonded elements in a fixed ratio.

text: Which change of state is deposition?
scheme: Deposition describes gas changing directly to solid.

text: A liquid mixture has two components with different boiling points. Which method is most appropriate?
scheme: Distillation separates miscible liquids according to their boiling behaviours.

text: Which state symbol represents a substance dissolved in water?
scheme: (aq) means aqueous: dissolved in water.

text: Distinguish an element, a compound and a mixture.
scheme: Element cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances [1].
Compound contains different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio [1].
Mixture contains substances not chemically bonded in no fixed ratio [1].

text: State how a solid dissolved in a liquid could be recovered and justify the method.
scheme: Identify evaporation or recrystallization as a relevant method [1].
Explain that solvent is removed or crystals form from the solution [1].
Recognize that the solute is recovered by a physical separation rather than chemical change [1].

text: A heating curve rises, becomes flat, then rises again. Explain the temperature plateau using the kinetic molecular model.
scheme: The sample is undergoing a change of state [1].
Energy is used to overcome/interact with attractions rather than increasing average kinetic energy [1].
Therefore the temperature remains constant during the change [1].

text: Convert 25.0 °C to kelvin. Explain what kelvin temperature measures.
scheme: Kelvin temperature measures average particle kinetic energy [1].

text: A neutral atom contains 13 protons and 14 neutrons. Its mass number is
scheme: A = protons + neutrons = 27.

text: An ion has atomic number 17 and charge −1. How many electrons does it have?
scheme: An extra electron produces a −1 charge: 17 + 1 = 18.

text: Isotopes of an element have different numbers of
scheme: Isotopes have the same number of protons and different neutron counts.

text: In a mass spectrum of a singly charged element, peaks at m/z 10 and 11 have abundances 20% and 80%. What is Aᵣ?
A species has A = 39, Z = 19 and charge +1. Determine its protons, neutrons and electrons.
scheme: 19 protons [1].
20 neutrons [1].
18 electrons [1].

text: An element has isotopes of masses 63 and 65, with abundances 69% and 31%. Calculate its relative atomic mass.
scheme: Use weighted mean with correct mass and percentage terms [1].

text: Explain how a mass spectrum can be used to determine relative atomic mass.
scheme: Identify isotopic mass from peak position [1].
Identify relative abundance from peak intensity [1].
Calculate weighted mean of isotopic masses [1].

text: Explain why isotopes can differ in physical properties despite being atoms of the same element.
scheme: They have different neutron numbers and masses [1].
Mass differences can affect physical behaviour [1].

text: What is the maximum number of electrons in the n = 3 main energy level?
Which statement correctly describes an orbital?
options: A region with high probability of finding an electron
scheme: Orbitals represent probable electron locations.

text: Which rule explains why electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly before pairing?
scheme: Hund’s rule favours singly occupied orbitals first.

text: Which light has the greatest photon energy?
scheme: E = hc/λ, so smaller wavelength corresponds to greater energy.

text: What is the general first-ionization-energy trend down a group?
options: Increases due to greater nuclear charge only
Decreases due to increased shielding and radius
Increases because electrons get closer to the nucleus
scheme: Greater atomic radius and shielding generally make electron removal easier.

text: Large jump between the third and fourth successive ionization energies suggests how many valence electrons?
scheme: The first three electrons are removed from the outer level before a core electron.

text: Describe three principles used to construct electron configurations.
scheme: Aufbau: lower energy orbitals fill before higher [1].
Hund: equivalent orbitals singly occupied before pairing [1].
Pauli: maximum two opposite-spin electrons per orbital [1].

text: Explain how a hydrogen line spectrum supports the idea of quantized energy.
scheme: The spectrum has discrete wavelengths/lines rather than a continuous spectrum [1].
These correspond to transitions between fixed electron energy levels [1].

text: A spectral convergence limit is observed at frequency 3.29 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Calculate energy of a photon using h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
scheme: Correct substitution E = hf [1].
2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per photon [1].

text: Explain the overall pattern and two discontinuities in first ionization energies across a period.
scheme: Effective nuclear attraction generally increases across a period [1].
Hence first ionization energy generally increases [1].
An electron entering a higher-energy p sublevel can produce a decrease [1].
Pairing in an orbital produces additional repulsion and can produce another decrease [1].

text: Write the condensed electron configuration of chlorine (Z = 17) and state the number of occupied p orbitals in its outer shell.
scheme: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵ [1].
Three outer 3p orbitals occupied [1].

text: Give the ground-state configurations of Cr (Z = 24) and Cu (Z = 29) and explain why these are exceptions to a simple filling pattern.
scheme: Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ [1].
Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ [1].
Relative stability associated with half-filled and filled 3d subshells [1].

text: What is the amount of 18.0 g of water (M = 18.0 g mol⁻¹)?
What is the molecular formula of a compound with empirical formula CH₂ and molar mass 56.0 g mol⁻¹? (C = 12, H = 1)
scheme: Empirical formula mass 14; multiplier 56/14 = 4.

text: What volume of a 0.200 mol dm⁻³ solution contains 0.0500 mol of solute?
At identical temperature and pressure, 20 cm³ gas A and 60 cm³ gas B have mole ratio
scheme: Avogadro’s law makes mole ratio equal gas volume ratio.

text: Calculate the molar mass of CaCO₃ using Ca = 40.08, C = 12.01, O = 16.00.
scheme: Include one Ca, one C and three O atoms [1].

text: A compound consists of 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass. Determine its empirical formula. Use C = 12.0, H = 1.0, O = 16.0.
scheme: Assume a 100 g sample [1].
Calculate moles: C ≈ 3.33; H = 6.7; O ≈ 3.33 [1].
Divide by the smallest amounts to obtain ≈1:2:1 [1].
CH₂O [1].

text: Calculate the molar concentration of a solution containing 0.120 mol of dissolved solute in 400 cm³ of solution.
scheme: Convert 400 cm³ to 0.400 dm³ [1].

text: A gas reaction is 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g). What volume of oxygen reacts with 80 cm³ CO at the same T and P?
scheme: Mole ratio CO:O₂ = 2:1 [1].
Gas volume ratio equals mole ratio under equal T and P [1].
40 cm³ O₂ [1].

text: State the difference between relative formula mass Mᵣ and molar mass M.
scheme: Mᵣ is relative and has no units [1].
M is mass per mole with units g mol⁻¹ [1].

text: Which is an assumption of an ideal gas?
scheme: The ideal gas model assumes elastic collisions.

text: When do real gases generally deviate most from ideal behaviour?
scheme: Low T increases importance of attractions, high P increases finite-volume effects.

text: At fixed T and fixed amount, pressure doubles. How does ideal gas volume change?
scheme: PV is constant for a fixed n and T.

text: Which SI pressure unit should be used with R in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ in PV = nRT?
scheme: Use pascal and cubic metres with the SI gas constant.

text: Explain why an ideal gas model becomes less accurate at low temperatures and high pressures.
scheme: Intermolecular attractions become more significant at low temperatures [1].
Molecular volume is no longer negligible at high pressure [1].
Both violate assumptions of the ideal-gas model [1].

text: Calculate the pressure of 0.200 mol of ideal gas at 300 K occupying 0.00500 m³. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
scheme: PV = nRT [1].
Rearrange P = nRT/V [1].

text: A fixed amount of ideal gas has volume 2.00 dm³ at 300 K. At the same pressure, determine volume at 450 K.
scheme: V/T constant at fixed pressure and n [1].

text: State two assumptions of an ideal gas model.
scheme: Negligible particle volume [1].
No intermolecular forces / elastic collisions [1].

text: What forms when a metal atom loses an electron?
scheme: Electron loss produces a positively charged ion.

text: What is the formula of magnesium phosphate? (Mg²⁺; PO₄³⁻)
scheme: Three Mg²⁺ and two PO₄³⁻ ions give total zero charge.

text: Which formula represents nitrate?
scheme: Nitrate is NO₃⁻.

text: Why can molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
options: Mobile electrons in the solid lattice
The nuclei can move through the solid
scheme: Mobile ions carry charge in the molten state.

text: Explain ionic bonding and why ionic solids have relatively high melting points.
scheme: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between opposite ions [1].
Ionic compounds have a giant three-dimensional lattice [1].
Significant energy is needed to overcome strong attractions [1].

text: Explain electrical conductivity of an ionic compound as solid, molten and aqueous solution.
scheme: Solid contains ions fixed in a lattice [1].
So the solid does not conduct [1].
Molten and aqueous forms contain mobile ions [1].
Mobile ions transport electrical charge [1].

text: Predict how increasing ionic charge and decreasing ionic radius affect lattice enthalpy magnitude.
scheme: Greater ion charge leads to stronger electrostatic attraction [1].
Smaller ion radius allows ions to approach more closely [1].
Both generally increase lattice enthalpy magnitude / ionic bonding strength [1].

text: Deduce the empirical formula of aluminium sulfate using Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻.
scheme: Charges balance with two Al³⁺ and three SO₄²⁻ [1].
Al₂(SO₄)₃ [1].

text: A triple covalent bond contains how many shared electron pairs?
scheme: A triple bond consists of three shared electron pairs.

text: Which molecular shape is predicted for a central atom with four bonding domains and no lone pairs?
scheme: Four domains adopt a tetrahedral electron arrangement and molecular shape.

text: Which statement correctly describes molecular polarity?
options: Any polar bond makes the molecule polar
Bond dipoles can cancel depending on geometry
scheme: Net dipole depends on the sum of bond dipoles and their directions.

text: Which arrangement has three electron domains around a central atom?
scheme: Three electron domains have trigonal planar electron-domain geometry.

text: Which interaction is generally strongest for comparable molar masses?
scheme: The syllabus gives hydrogen bonding as strongest among these under comparable molar masses.

text: A chromatography spot travels 3.0 cm and the solvent front travels 7.5 cm. What is Rf?
Which carbon allotrope has delocalized electrons within planar layers?
scheme: Graphite has delocalized electrons within its carbon layers.

text: How many π bonds are in a carbon–carbon triple bond?
scheme: A triple bond contains one σ and two π bonds.

text: What is the electron-domain geometry of five domains around a central atom?
scheme: Five electron domains correspond to trigonal bipyramidal geometry.

text: Which hybridization corresponds to two electron domains?
scheme: Two domains correspond to sp hybridization.

text: A neutral atom has five valence electrons, one non-bonding pair and three single bonds. What is its formal charge?
Which observation supports electron delocalization in benzene?
options: Alternating distinct long and short C–C bonds
Equal C–C bond lengths around the ring
scheme: Equal ring C–C lengths are consistent with delocalized bonding.

text: Define a covalent bond and explain the octet rule.
scheme: Electrostatic attraction between shared electron pair and positive nuclei [1].
Octet rule concerns achieving eight electrons in the valence shell [1].
Recognize the rule has exceptions such as incomplete octets [1].

text: State the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry of NH₃, and explain the difference.
scheme: Four domains give tetrahedral electron-domain geometry [1].
Three bonds and one lone pair give trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry [1].
Molecular geometry describes atom positions, not lone-pair positions [1].

text: Explain why CO₂ has polar bonds but no overall permanent dipole moment.
scheme: C=O bonds are polar because the atoms differ in electronegativity [1].
CO₂ is linear and symmetrical [1].
Equal bond dipoles cancel [1].

text: Compare the bonding and conductivity of diamond and graphite.
scheme: Diamond is a three-dimensional network of covalently bonded carbon atoms [1].
Graphite has extended sheets/layers with delocalized electrons [1].
Graphite conducts along layers; diamond normally does not due to absent mobile charge carriers [1].

text: Explain the relative boiling temperatures of two similarly sized molecules, one capable of hydrogen bonding and one with only dispersion forces.
scheme: Identify hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular interaction [1].
Identify London dispersion in both molecules [1].
Hydrogen bonding is generally stronger under comparable molar masses [1].
More energy is required to separate molecules, leading to higher boiling temperature [1].

text: In a chromatography experiment a spot moves 2.4 cm and the solvent front moves 6.0 cm. Calculate Rf and interpret a low Rf.
scheme: Rf = distance spot / distance solvent front [1].
Lower Rf reflects relatively stronger stationary-phase attraction (under the given conditions) [1].

text: Distinguish London dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding interactions.
scheme: London dispersion results from temporary/induced dipoles and occurs in all molecules [1].
Dipole–dipole interactions act between permanent dipoles [1].
Hydrogen bonding is an attractive interaction involving H covalently attached to a strongly electronegative atom and a neighbouring electronegative atom [1].

text: Explain why a molecule with a central atom bonded to two atoms may be bent instead of linear.
scheme: Count electron domains around the central atom [1].
Non-bonding electron pairs repel bonding pairs [1].
Lone pairs affect the positions of bonds and reduce their bond angle relative to the ideal arrangement [1].

text: Explain resonance in benzene using bonding and structural evidence.
scheme: More than one localized double-bond arrangement can be drawn [1].
Actual π electrons are delocalized around the ring [1].
Equal C–C bond lengths support delocalization [1].

text: Determine the formal charge on oxygen in a Lewis structure with two lone pairs and a double bond.
scheme: O has six valence electrons [1].
Four non-bonding electrons and four bonding electrons (half allocated) [1].

text: Explain sigma and pi bonds in ethene, C₂H₄, and give the total number of each.
scheme: A sigma bond involves head-on overlap [1].
A pi bond involves lateral p-orbital overlap [1].
Ethene contains five σ bonds (four C–H and one C–C) [1].
Ethene contains one π bond [1].

text: Compare the hybridization and molecular geometry around each carbon in ethene and ethyne.
scheme: Both carbon atoms in ethene are sp², trigonal planar [1].
Both carbon atoms in ethyne are sp, linear [1].
Relate differences to three versus two electron domains [1].

text: Determine the electron-domain geometry for a central atom with six domains, including two lone pairs, and explain why its molecular geometry differs.
scheme: Six domains yield octahedral electron-domain geometry [1].
Molecular geometry depends on the positions of bonded atoms only [1].
Two lone pairs occupy domains but are excluded from the molecular-shape description [1].

text: An ion has two valid Lewis contributors with a double bond in alternative positions. Explain the implication for its bonding.
scheme: Identify resonance contributors [1].
Identify delocalized electrons rather than a fixed single localized double bond [1].
Explain that atom positions stay unchanged while electron arrangement differs [1].

text: A nitrogen atom has five valence electrons, zero lone pairs and four single bonds in a Lewis structure. Determine its formal charge.
scheme: FC = valence − nonbonding − ½ bonding electrons [1].
